concept_families.family_claim: The ordinary pressure is Handle a speaker moving between languages within an utterance, including pronunciation, grammar, and word-boundary changes. In the reviewed evidence, the family appears as SpokenNativQA: Multilingual Everyday Spoken Queries for LLMs: Everyday multilingual spoken queries test whether a language model handles language choice and meaning together instead of translating an artificial sentence list.; From Context to Code-switching: Examining the Interplay of Language Proficiency and Multilingualism in Speech: The study connects code-switching behavior to language background and proficiency, showing why multilingual speech cannot be interpreted without speaker and language context.; Adapting Whisper for low-resource Hindi-English Code-Mix speech with on-the-fly Augmentation & LLM-Synthesised Data: The method combines language prompts and code-mixed augmentation, so the core problem is switching language systems within speech rather than generic multilingual scaling. It must not be confused with neighboring problems outside this boundary: A monolingual metric can count appropriate switching as error and fail to define the intended transcript.
concept_families.unresolved: Whether this concept remains useful outside the reviewed speakers, languages, devices, rooms, and tasks is unresolved; 5 D3 paper(s) provide full-paper evidence.

records.subtheme_name: Learning when labels and recordings are scarce
records.question: How can a system improve without assuming a large clean labeled corpus?

family_synthesis.ordinary_pressure: Languages differ in sounds, writing systems, grammar, prosody, code-switching, and social meaning; data and tools are distributed unevenly. The subtheme asks: How can a system improve without assuming a large clean labeled corpus?
family_synthesis.naive_shortcut: A first attempt would answer the question only with self-training, but that shortcut misses the boundary: Errors can reinforce themselves and create a false appearance of data scale.
family_synthesis.recurring_move: Across this subtheme, papers make self-training, speech data collection, few-shot adaptation explicit rather than treating the speech evidence as one undifferentiated variable. The reviewed full-paper mechanisms instantiate that move in different ways; for example: Continue pretraining a compact HuBERT-style model on a much wider set of African-language audio, then test whether the shared representation transfers to downstream tasks.
subtheme_boundary: Errors can reinforce themselves and create a false appearance of data scale.
More hours do not fix biased sampling, poor transcripts, or a task definition that excludes natural speech.
Few examples may cover only one speaker or style and make variance look like progress.
family_synthesis.tradeoff: The recurring move must preserve the evidence relevant to the named concept without importing a neighboring concept's assumptions; the boundaries below state where that interpretation stops.
family_synthesis.reviewed_variation: AfriHuBERT: A self-supervised speech representation model for African languages: The paper expands self-supervised pretraining across African languages so useful speech units can be learned where labeled data are scarce.; Evaluating Large Language Models in Data Generation for Low-Resource Scenarios: A Case Study on Question Answering: Low-resource speech generation asks whether artificial examples teach a recognizer the missing variation or merely repeat the generator's assumptions.; Better Semi-supervised Learning for Multi-domain ASR Through Incremental Retraining and Data Filtering: The captured paper's ordinary problem, mechanism, and reported evaluation directly instantiate self-training-and-pseudo-labels within low-resource-and-data-creation.; MSDA: Combining Pseudo-labeling and Self-Supervision for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in ASR: Unsupervised ASR adaptation uses pseudo-labels and self-supervision when target transcripts are scarce, but must filter errors before they reinforce themselves.
d3_mechanism_evidence: Continue pretraining a compact HuBERT-style model on a much wider set of African-language audio, then test whether the shared representation transfers to downstream tasks.
Use large-language-model-generated question-answer data and test its value separately on text QA, spoken QA, and Turkish spoken QA.
Incrementally combine in-domain labels with related-domain data, then filter pseudo-labels using multi-model consensus or named-entity recognition.
Cascade self-supervised representation adaptation with pseudo-label training so each stage prepares the next.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: AfriHuBERT: A self-supervised speech representation model for African languages
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Continue pretraining a compact HuBERT-style model on a much wider set of African-language audio, then test whether the shared representation transfers to downstream tasks.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Unlabeled audio is converted into masked prediction targets; the encoder learns from contextual speech patterns across languages and is then adapted for recognition and language-related tasks.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We evaluate AfriHuBERT on two key speech tasks, Spoken Language Identification (SLID) and Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), using the FLEURS benchmark.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports a representation model expanded to 1,226 African languages and evaluates its transfer against multilingual baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports a representation model expanded to 1,226 African languages and evaluates its transfer against multilingual baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Language coverage does not mean equal data quality or equal downstream performance; the languages, hours, speaker balance, and task results determine the practical reach. No independent reproduction was performed.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Data Generation for Low-Resource Scenarios: A Case Study on Question Answering
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Use large-language-model-generated question-answer data and test its value separately on text QA, spoken QA, and Turkish spoken QA.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The study evaluates LLM-generated data for low-resource spoken QA across SQuAD, Spoken SQuAD, and Turkish spoken QA.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful tools for generating synthetic data, offering a promising solution to data scarcity in low-resource scenarios.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports relative F1 gains over restricted human-annotated training in the tested text and spoken QA settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports relative F1 gains over restricted human-annotated training in the tested text and spoken QA settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Prompting, filtering, language, synthetic distribution, and evaluation splits limit transfer; synthetic gains do not establish factual or linguistic quality everywhere.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Better Semi-supervised Learning for Multi-domain ASR Through Incremental Retraining and Data Filtering
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Incrementally combine in-domain labels with related-domain data, then filter pseudo-labels using multi-model consensus or named-entity recognition.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The pipeline retrains in stages and uses agreement or entity preservation to decide which generated transcripts enter the next training round.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We propose an incremental semi-supervised learning pipeline that first integrates a small in-domain labeled set and an auxiliary dataset from a closely related domain, achieving a relative improvement of 4% over no auxiliary data.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports up to 22.3% relative improvement on Wow and 24.8% on Fisher over random selection, with consensus strongest and NER cheaper.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports up to 22.3% relative improvement on Wow and 24.8% on Fisher over random selection, with consensus strongest and NER cheaper.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The gains are bounded to the two English corpora, model ensemble, filtering thresholds, and author-reported WER; other domains and languages remain unresolved.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: MSDA: Combining Pseudo-labeling and Self-Supervision for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in ASR
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Cascade self-supervised representation adaptation with pseudo-label training so each stage prepares the next.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: MSDA evaluates a two-stage Meta PL pipeline for Greek and weakly supervised ASR, with ablations of the cascade.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: MSDA is evaluated for six source-to-target Greek domain transfers using target-domain WER, comparing supervised source fine-tuning, continual pretraining, M2DS2, Meta pseudo-labeling, CASTLE, and MSDA. The corpora include 72-hour Logotypografia, 12-hour Common Voice, 99-hour HParl, and weakly supervised Greek Podcast subsets, with greedy decoding in the reported table.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports state-of-the-art results and finds the cascading combination necessary in its experiments.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports state-of-the-art results and finds the cascading combination necessary in its experiments.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The languages, pseudo-label quality, source models, and domain shifts bound the claim; robustness to severely wrong pseudo-labels remains open.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Speechless: Speech Instruction Training Without Speech for Low Resource Languages
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Generate synthetic instruction examples only up to a semantic representation, align those representations with a pretrained speech encoder, and train the language model without waveform synthesis.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Speechless uses text-generated instructions, aligns their semantic representations with Whisper encoder representations, and fine-tunes an LLM so it can process spoken commands in low-resource settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: The rapid growth of voice assistants powered by large language models (LLM) has highlighted a need for speech instruction data to train these systems.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports that speech-instruction training without TTS can preserve spoken-instruction understanding and offers a simpler route for low-resource languages.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports that speech-instruction training without TTS can preserve spoken-instruction understanding and offers a simpler route for low-resource languages.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The language, synthetic text, Whisper encoder, alignment quality, and downstream command tasks bound the result; semantic alignment is not proof that pronunciation, prosody, or real user speech are fully represented.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Nosey: Open-Source Hardware for Acoustic Nasalance
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build open hardware whose microphone, baffle, and analog path can be changed, then compare raw scores and phonological contrasts against a commercial device.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Nosey is a 3-D-printable baffle with replaceable dual microphone clips and open files; the study compares it with an icSpeech device for speakers and phonological environments.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We also review ways of customizing the hardware to facilitate testing, such as comparison of microphones and different construction materials.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Nosey produces consistently higher raw nasalance scores, but preserves comparable phonological-environment contrasts under the tested conditions and offers a lower-cost customizable platform.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Nosey produces consistently higher raw nasalance scores, but preserves comparable phonological-environment contrasts under the tested conditions and offers a lower-cost customizable platform.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The tested speakers, microphones, baffle geometry, placement, and phonological materials bound the comparison; raw-score offsets and cross-signal bleed prevent treating Nosey and commercial values as directly interchangeable.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Transcribing Oral History Recordings Using the Transcription Portal
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Put recognition, human correction, and export into one preconfigured web workflow designed around the user's task rather than the model's internals.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The Transcription Portal provides a GUI with three steps—ASR, manual correction, and data export—supports several languages, and demonstrates the workflow on historical Italian Ravensbrück interviews.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: The Transcription Portal workflow is demonstrated on four 1976 Italian oral-history interviews with five Ravensbrück survivors and approximately 18 hours of speech digitized at 96 kHz/24-bit. Evaluation is a bounded transcription-workflow demonstration comparing ASR-generated SRT material with manual correction and export, not a held-out WER experiment; corpus access and editor operations are the evidence objects.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports a usable multilingual portal and demonstrates it on oral-history recordings, with summarization and translation identified as future extensions.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports a usable multilingual portal and demonstrates it on oral-history recordings, with summarization and translation identified as future extensions.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The demonstration corpus, user effort, ASR model, correction time, and export format bound the result; a convenient workflow does not establish transcription accuracy without an error audit or independent user study.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: The NaijaVoices Dataset: Cultivating Large-Scale, High-Quality, Culturally-Rich Speech Data for African Languages
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Collect a large, culturally grounded speech-text corpus and test whether it improves several ASR families.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: NaijaVoices contains 1,800 hours from more than 5,000 speakers; the paper analyzes acoustic diversity and fine-tunes Whisper, MMS, and XLSR.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: The development of high-performing, robust, and reliable speech technologies depends on large, high-quality datasets.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports average WER improvements of 75.86% for Whisper, 52.06% for MMS, and 42.33% for XLSR.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports average WER improvements of 75.86% for Whisper, 52.06% for MMS, and 42.33% for XLSR.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The corpus languages, collection process, transcription policy, and model choices bound the result; coverage of other African languages and deployment conditions remains open.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Multi-view Fusion and Parameter Perturbation for Few-Shot Class-Incremental Audio Classification
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Fuse multiple views of the audio and perturb parameters during few-shot class-incremental learning to improve coverage and reduce overfitting.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper proposes multi-view fusion and parameter perturbation for few-shot class-incremental audio classification.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Extensive evaluations on two widely-used audio datasets, NS-100 and LS-100, demonstrate that MVF2P outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of average accuracy and performance drop rate.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports class-incremental classification results against the tested baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports class-incremental classification results against the tested baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Class order, shots, audio domains, perturbation settings, and memory protocol bound the result; benchmark retention does not establish lifelong robustness.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Speech LLMs in Low-Resource Scenarios: Data Volume Requirements and the Impact of Pretraining on High-Resource Languages
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Pretrain the small bridge between a speech encoder and language model on high-resource languages, then reuse it and measure how much low-resource data is still needed.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Using SLAM-ASR with Whisper-large-v3-turbo and multilingual or monolingual LLMs, the paper varies training volume and projector pretraining, including Galician benchmarks.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Using multilingual LLMs (EuroLLM, Salamandra) with whisper-large-v3-turbo, we evaluate performance on several public benchmarks, providing insights for future research on optimizing Speech LLMs for low-resource languages and multilinguality.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports that multilingual projector pretraining reduces the impact of scarce data; for Galician it reports WERs such as 13.3% on Common Voice and 19.4% on FLEURS in one configuration.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports that multilingual projector pretraining reduces the impact of scarce data; for Galician it reports WERs such as 13.3% on Common Voice and 19.4% on FLEURS in one configuration.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Language choice, data cleanliness, projector, LLM, benchmark split, and WER bound the claim; transfer from high-resource languages does not establish equal performance or cultural adequacy.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Evaluating Wav2Vec2-Bert for Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training for isiZulu
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Compare Wav2Vec2-BERT models fine-tuned on native isiZulu, learner speech, and both, then evaluate transcription and phoneme-error detection separately.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The study uses NCHLT native speech, L2 isiZulu learner speech, and teacher recordings. Models are fine-tuned with the same setup; phoneme alignment uses Needleman–Wunsch, and error labels are evaluated with false acceptance, false rejection, and true-negative rates.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Through creating and evaluating three fine-tuned versions of Wav2Vec2-Bert, this paper investigates the performance of Wav2Vec2-Bert for detecting language learner errors in low-resource settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Native-speech transcription is strongest for the NCHLT-trained model, while the L2-trained model detects the most incorrect phonemes under the available true-negative measure; the authors release code and identify the data sources.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Native-speech transcription is strongest for the NCHLT-trained model, while the L2-trained model detects the most incorrect phonemes under the available true-negative measure; the authors release code and identify the data sources.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The results depend on three isiZulu corpora, their recording styles, and incomplete phoneme-error labels. Tone is not evaluated because it is not marked orthographically; findings do not automatically transfer to other languages or pronunciation tasks.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Few-Shot Speech Deepfake Detection Adaptation with Gaussian Processes
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Use Gaussian-process adaptation to express uncertainty and update the detector from scarce examples.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper studies few-shot adaptation for speech deepfake detection with Gaussian processes.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We show how the combination of a powerful deep embedding model with the Gaussian processes flexibility can achieve strong performance and adaptability.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports few-shot detection adaptation results against the tested baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports few-shot detection adaptation results against the tested baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Attack families, kernel choices, calibration, shots, and base detector limit generalization; uncertainty estimates are not automatically reliable under distribution shift.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Pushing the Limits of Beam Search Decoding  for Transducer-based ASR models
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Analyze and improve beam-search decoding for transducer ASR, testing how search choices affect accuracy and computation.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper pushes the limits of beam-search decoding for transducer-based ASR models.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Transducer models have emerged as a promising choice for end-to-end ASR systems, offering a balanced trade-off between recognition accuracy, streaming capabilities, and inference speed in greedy decoding.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports decoding accuracy and efficiency findings for transducer ASR across the tested search settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports decoding accuracy and efficiency findings for transducer ASR across the tested search settings.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Model, language, beam policy, pruning, hardware, and streaming setup bound the result; a better beam does not remove acoustic or language-model errors.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Automatic Speech Recognition for Low-Resourced Middle Eastern Languages
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build and evaluate ASR resources for low-resourced Middle Eastern languages, making language-specific data and transfer limits explicit.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper studies automatic speech recognition for low-resourced Middle Eastern languages.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Low-resource ASR is evaluated on held-out parallel-corpus test sentences for six Middle Eastern languages, with remaining recordings used for training and validation merged into training. Untuned Whisper Base/Small zero-shot baselines are compared with multilingual and monolingual fine-tuning using WER and CER; results include 1,000-bootstrap significance tests (200 for Zazaki), with monolingual mean WER 64.4 versus multilingual 60.5 and language-specific outcomes reported by language.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports resources, baselines, and recognition results for the covered Middle Eastern languages.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports resources, baselines, and recognition results for the covered Middle Eastern languages.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Language selection, dialect, corpus size, transcription, speakers, and evaluation splits limit generalization across the region.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: An Effective Training Framework for Light-Weight Automatic Speech Recognition Models
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Design a training framework that improves lightweight ASR while measuring the accuracy-resource tradeoff directly.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper proposes an effective training framework for lightweight automatic speech-recognition models.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Comprehensive experimentation on ASR benchmarks reveals the efficacy of our approach, achieving three-fold training speed-up and up to 12.54% word error rate improvement.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports lightweight ASR accuracy and resource results for the proposed framework.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports lightweight ASR accuracy and resource results for the proposed framework.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Hardware, language, model family, data, latency measurement, and compression settings limit generalization; a benchmark model is not a deployment guarantee.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Hybrid Data Sampling for ASR: Integrating Acoustic Diversity and Transcription Uncertainty
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Combine acoustic-diversity measures with transcription uncertainty when selecting training data, then test the effect on ASR.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper proposes hybrid data sampling for ASR by integrating acoustic diversity and transcription uncertainty.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We evaluate our method on Japanese speech datasets, CSJ and ReazonSpeech, demonstrating that it achieves lower recognition error rates than random or single-criterion-based data selection.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports ASR improvements from hybrid sampling relative to the tested selection strategies.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports ASR improvements from hybrid sampling relative to the tested selection strategies.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Acoustic representation, uncertainty estimator, corpus, budget, language, and split bound the result; a sampling score is not a complete measure of data value.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: An Exploratory Framework for LLM-assisted Human Annotation of Speech Datasets
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build an exploratory human-in-the-loop framework for LLM-assisted speech annotation with review, uncertainty, and provenance.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper presents an exploratory framework for LLM-assisted human annotation of speech datasets.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We introduce a framework for LLM-based human-in-the-loop ASR designed to enhance the quality of ASR transcripts, with a particular focus on accurately capturing named entities.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports framework behavior and exploratory annotation findings for the tested speech data tasks.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports framework behavior and exploratory annotation findings for the tested speech data tasks.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Task, annotator expertise, model, prompts, disagreement policy, and audit trail bound the result; assistance is not a substitute for label validity.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Speech Annotation for A: Accuracy, Access, and Application
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Keep the model-generated draft but make human correction cheap: edit in synchronized chunks, highlight every difference, tag speaker/language explicitly, and export structured research files.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: SAFA combines Whisper and diarization drafts with a PyQt6 interface. Chunk navigation follows playback, original and edited text/tags/timestamps are compared in real time, language and speaker labels are selectable, and CSV/SRT/TXT exports preserve the corrected record.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: By pairing annotation drafts generated from large language models with chunk-based editing, real-time difference highlighting, and speaker & language tagging - even in multi-speaker code-switching scenarios - SAFA delivers high-quality audio annotations ready for research with minimal setup and minimal human check.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper presents an end-to-end bilingual clinical annotation workflow intended to reduce setup and manual effort while retaining human validation and structured metadata for downstream research.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper presents an end-to-end bilingual clinical annotation workflow intended to reduce setup and manual effort while retaining human validation and structured metadata for downstream research.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The paper does not report a controlled user study, annotation-time reduction, inter-annotator agreement, or clinical outcome. Whisper/diarization errors and supported language choices remain boundaries; tool availability is not independent execution.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: The Faetar Speech Recognition Benchmark
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build the Faetar speech-recognition benchmark with documented recordings, splits, transcripts, and evaluation so later systems can be compared on the same problem.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper introduces the Faetar Speech Recognition Benchmark.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We introduce the Faetar Automatic Speech Recognition Benchmark, a benchmark corpus designed to push the limits of current approaches to low-resource speech recognition.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports the benchmark resources and baseline recognition results for Faetar.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports the benchmark resources and baseline recognition results for Faetar.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Corpus size, speakers, dialect coverage, transcription conventions, and split design bound conclusions about the wider language community.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: LiRI Corpus Platform: Demonstration of a Web-Based Infrastructure for Multimodal Corpus Analysis
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Provide one corpus platform with a shared query language, synchronized audiovisual views, and layered annotation that can be queried across modalities.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The LiRI Corpus Platform stores and explores multimodal corpora through DQD queries and time-aligned frontends for text, audio, video, gesture, and spoken transcripts.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We present the LiRI Corpus Platform (LCP), a web-based infrastructure for storing, exploring, and analyzing diverse linguistic corpora with a focus on multimodal and audiovisual data.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper demonstrates integrated storage, synchronized querying, layered annotation, and modality-specific frontends for multimodal corpus analysis.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper demonstrates integrated storage, synchronized querying, layered annotation, and modality-specific frontends for multimodal corpus analysis.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: This is an infrastructure demonstration, not evidence that every corpus can be aligned or that research conclusions improve; supported formats, annotations, and user workflows are the boundary.

family_synthesis.comparison_conclusion: The papers share the ordinary pressure but intervene at different points in the chain; their reported outcomes are not directly rankable unless the measured object and test condition match.
family_synthesis.named_contrast: AfriHuBERT: A self-supervised speech representation model for African languages versus Evaluating Large Language Models in Data Generation for Low-Resource Scenarios: A Case Study on Question Answering
family_synthesis.mechanism_contrast: AfriHuBERT: A self-supervised speech representation model for African languages addresses the pressure by Unlabeled audio is converted into masked prediction targets; the encoder learns from contextual speech patterns across languages and is then adapted for recognition and language-related tasks.; Evaluating Large Language Models in Data Generation for Low-Resource Scenarios: A Case Study on Question Answering addresses it by The study evaluates LLM-generated data for low-resource spoken QA across SQuAD, Spoken SQuAD, and Turkish spoken QA.. The shared problem is therefore compatible with more than one intervention point.
family_synthesis.evidence_contrast: The first paper reports The paper reports a representation model expanded to 1,226 African languages and evaluates its transfer against multilingual baselines.; the second reports The paper reports relative F1 gains over restricted human-annotated training in the tested text and spoken QA settings.. These outcomes should not be ranked unless their data, listeners, metric, and test condition are comparable.
family_synthesis.failure_boundary_contrast: The first paper leaves open: Language coverage does not mean equal data quality or equal downstream performance; the languages, hours, speaker balance, and task results determine the practical reach. No independent reproduction was performed.; the second leaves open: Prompting, filtering, language, synthetic distribution, and evaluation splits limit transfer; synthetic gains do not establish factual or linguistic quality everywhere.. Those are evidence boundaries, not proof that either method fails outside the paper.
family_synthesis.transfer_question: What would have to remain invariant for this family to work across a new speaker, language, room, device, or task, and which paper evidence here actually tests that transfer?
family_synthesis.evidence_boundary: The shared story is supported only by the reviewed papers listed here; D2 entries support the problem and stated method, while D3 entries support the reported mechanism and evaluation. It is not a venue-wide prevalence claim.
family_synthesis.unresolved_question: What changes when this move is tested outside the speakers, languages, rooms, devices, or benchmark conditions represented by the 20 D3 paper(s)?

concept_families.definition: Design recording prompts, speakers, transcription, and consent so newly collected data covers the intended community and task.
concept_families.boundary: More hours do not fix biased sampling, poor transcripts, or a task definition that excludes natural speech.
concept_families.family_claim: The ordinary pressure is Design recording prompts, speakers, transcription, and consent so newly collected data covers the intended community and task. In the reviewed evidence, the family appears as Nosey: Open-Source Hardware for Acoustic Nasalance: An open acoustic-nasalance device changes what can be collected about speech, connecting low-cost hardware to new clinical and language resources.; Transcribing Oral History Recordings Using the Transcription Portal: Oral-history transcription must adapt tools and review practices to long, noisy, historically varied recordings.; The NaijaVoices Dataset: Cultivating Large-Scale, High-Quality, Culturally-Rich Speech Data for African Languages: A culturally rich African-language dataset addresses unequal speech resources by changing who and which varieties are represented. It must not be confused with neighboring problems outside this boundary: More hours do not fix biased sampling, poor transcripts, or a task definition that excludes natural speech.
concept_families.unresolved: Whether this concept remains useful outside the reviewed speakers, languages, devices, rooms, and tasks is unresolved; 10 D3 paper(s) provide full-paper evidence.

concept_families.definition: Adjust a model to a language, speaker, or domain from a small number of examples rather than retraining from scratch.
concept_families.boundary: Few examples may cover only one speaker or style and make variance look like progress.
concept_families.family_claim: The ordinary pressure is Adjust a model to a language, speaker, or domain from a small number of examples rather than retraining from scratch. In the reviewed evidence, the family appears as Speechless: Speech Instruction Training Without Speech for Low Resource Languages: Low-resource languages need useful speech instruction without assuming large speech corpora; the method shifts supervision toward language and text resources.; Multi-view Fusion and Parameter Perturbation for Few-Shot Class-Incremental Audio Classification: Few-shot class-incremental audio learning must add new categories without erasing the old ones when labeled examples are scarce.; Evaluating Wav2Vec2-Bert for Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training for isiZulu: IsiZulu pronunciation assessment exposes how language-specific data and incomplete error labels limit the meaning of recognition scores. It must not be confused with neighboring problems outside this boundary: Few examples may cover only one speaker or style and make variance look like progress.

records.subtheme_name: Accent, dialect, and cultural interpretation
records.question: When is a difference a recognition problem, and when is it the system's narrow norm?

family_synthesis.ordinary_pressure: Languages differ in sounds, writing systems, grammar, prosody, code-switching, and social meaning; data and tools are distributed unevenly. The subtheme asks: When is a difference a recognition problem, and when is it the system's narrow norm?
family_synthesis.naive_shortcut: A first attempt would answer the question only with accent robustness, but that shortcut misses the boundary: A single pooled error rate cannot show which accents fail or whether adaptation changes identity representation.
family_synthesis.recurring_move: Across this subtheme, papers make accent robustness, dialect and variety, cultural meaning explicit rather than treating the speech evidence as one undifferentiated variable. The reviewed full-paper mechanisms instantiate that move in different ways; for example: Cross-examine /s/ production in a multilingual Nigerian context using linguistic and social context.
subtheme_boundary: A single pooled error rate cannot show which accents fail or whether adaptation changes identity representation.
Dialect labels can be contested and may conflate region, ethnicity, class, and speaker identity.
A label imported from another culture may be statistically convenient but semantically wrong.
family_synthesis.tradeoff: The recurring move must preserve the evidence relevant to the named concept without importing a neighboring concept's assumptions; the boundaries below state where that interpretation stops.
family_synthesis.reviewed_variation: Is it all about race?: A Cross-examination of /s/ in a Multilingual (Nigerian) Context: The paper measures /s/ variation across a multilingual Nigerian population and treats ethnicity, age, gender, and phonological context as boundaries on interpretation.; LID Models are Actually Accent Classifiers: Implications and Solutions for LID on Accented Speech: Language identification must preserve language evidence while refusing the shortcut that treats accent as language.; Accent Normalization Using Self-Supervised Discrete Tokens with Non-Parallel Data: Discrete tokens change pronunciation while preserving speaker identity with nonparallel accent data.; A Multi-Dialectal Dataset for German Dialect ASR and Dialect-to-Standard Speech Translation: A multi-dialect dataset makes German variety differences part of the recognition and translation target instead of normalizing them away.
d3_mechanism_evidence: Cross-examine /s/ production in a multilingual Nigerian context using linguistic and social context.
Add phoneme-sequence or discretized-unit views and test the shortcut by permuting short speech chunks.
Use self-supervised discrete tokens, nonparallel conversion, flow matching, and explicit duration preservation.
Create a multi-dialect benchmark with dialectal and Standard German transcriptions, then compare multilingual ASR systems on recognition and dialect-to-standard speech translation.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Is it all about race?: A Cross-examination of /s/ in a Multilingual (Nigerian) Context
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Cross-examine /s/ production in a multilingual Nigerian context using linguistic and social context.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Acoustic realization is interpreted alongside multilingual context rather than one norm.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: The analysis uses 4,056 /s/ tokens from 42 Nigerian English speakers across Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba groups. CoG, duration, skewness, and zero-crossing measures are analyzed with mixed-effects regressions using gender, birth year, segment duration, speaker, and phonological environment; reported effects are group- and predictor-specific rather than a recognition accuracy score.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports a contextual analysis of /s/ in a multilingual Nigerian setting.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports a contextual analysis of /s/ in a multilingual Nigerian setting.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Community, language, sampling, annotation, and interpretation bound transfer.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: LID Models are Actually Accent Classifiers: Implications and Solutions for LID on Accented Speech
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Add phoneme-sequence or discretized-unit views and test the shortcut by permuting short speech chunks.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The study compares ECAPA-TDNN, MMS, and GEO systems on several corpora, measures accent-language confusion, reverses chunks, and fuses acoustic and sequence representations.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Prior research indicates that LID model performance significantly declines on accented speech; however, the specific causes, extent, and characterization of these errors remain under-explored.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Dutch-accented English is called Dutch in 82.6% of errors in one setting; sequence-aware systems reduce this confusion while retaining mainstream performance.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Dutch-accented English is called Dutch in 82.6% of errors in one setting; sequence-aware systems reduce this confusion while retaining mainstream performance.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Datasets, accent categories, chunking, and aggregation define the result; it diagnoses a shortcut but does not prove cultural neutrality or universal transfer.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Accent Normalization Using Self-Supervised Discrete Tokens with Non-Parallel Data
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Use self-supervised discrete tokens, nonparallel conversion, flow matching, and explicit duration preservation.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The system extracts source tokens, predicts target-accent tokens, synthesizes waveform output, and evaluates several English accents.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Accent normalization is evaluated on seven accents from L2-ARCTIC/ARCTIC, with four speakers per accent, 50 validation and 80 held-out test sentences, and one unseen speaker per accent. WER, speaker-embedding cosine similarity, MUSHRA naturalness/accentedness, and best-worst speaker similarity are compared with a frame-to-frame baseline; subjective tests use 21 raters and 20 samples.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The system beats a frame-to-frame baseline on naturalness, accentedness, and timbre preservation, but post-conversion WER remains high.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The system beats a frame-to-frame baseline on naturalness, accentedness, and timbre preservation, but post-conversion WER remains high.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Accent definitions, targets, subjective judgments, and nonparallel training bound the claim; native-like is not universally better.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: A Multi-Dialectal Dataset for German Dialect ASR and Dialect-to-Standard Speech Translation
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Create a multi-dialect benchmark with dialectal and Standard German transcriptions, then compare multilingual ASR systems on recognition and dialect-to-standard speech translation.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The dataset crosses three Southeast German dialect groups and Standard German; paired transcription conventions make both recognition fidelity and normalization visible.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: To enable studies of how robust models are towards dialectal variation, we present Betthupferl, an evaluation dataset containing four hours of read speech in three dialect groups spoken in Southeast Germany (Franconian, Bavarian, Alemannic), and half an hour of Standard German speech.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Betthupferl provides four hours of dialect speech plus Standard German and reports model-dependent differences in recognition and translation behavior across dialect groups.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Betthupferl provides four hours of dialect speech plus Standard German and reports model-dependent differences in recognition and translation behavior across dialect groups.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Read speech, regional coverage, speaker sampling, benchmark size, and translation direction constrain the conclusions; dataset inclusion does not guarantee broad fairness or dialect preservation in deployed systems.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: The ML-SUPERB 2.0 Challenge: Towards Inclusive ASR Benchmarking for All Language Varieties
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build a broad public test suite and an online evaluation process that makes language-variety performance visible.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: ML-SUPERB 2.0 evaluates models on 200+ languages, accents, and dialects through DynaBench and compares five challenge submissions with baselines.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: We construct a new test suite that consists of data from 200+ languages, accents, and dialects to evaluate SOTA multilingual speech models.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The best submission reports 23% absolute LID improvement and 18% CER reduction generally, with 30.2% lower CER and 15.7% higher LID accuracy on accented/dialectal data.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The best submission reports 23% absolute LID improvement and 18% CER reduction generally, with 30.2% lower CER and 15.7% higher LID accuracy on accented/dialectal data.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Challenge submissions, test-suite composition, and hidden evaluation define the boundary; the results do not prove equal service quality for every language variety.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Tonal Variation and Word Meaning in Taiwanese
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Analyze spontaneous high-falling tone realizations while modeling word meaning and compare residual sandhi/citation differences.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Acoustic tone measurements are grouped by lexical/semantic context, allowing meaning-induced variation to be separated from categorical tone effects.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Tonal variation is analyzed on 4,294 high-falling-tone tokens from 16 Taiwan Southern Min speakers: 1,423 citation realizations and 2,871 sandhi realizations across 41 word types. F0 is sampled at 21 normalized time points and modeled with generalized additive models, with word meaning, tone type, speaker, and phonetic controls defining the comparison.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Word meaning explains part of tonal variability; after accounting for it, the reported sandhi/citation difference disappears.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Word meaning explains part of tonal variability; after accounting for it, the reported sandhi/citation difference disappears.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Speaker sample, spontaneous corpus, lexical items, tone context, and statistical model bound transfer; one tone pattern is not the whole Taiwanese system.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: ViToSA: Audio-Based Toxic Spans Detection on Vietnamese Speech Utterances
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Create an audio-based Vietnamese toxic-span task that preserves local evidence and evaluates both detection and boundary selection.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: ViToSA builds an audio dataset and task for locating toxic spans in Vietnamese speech utterances.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: This paper introduces ViToSA (Vietnamese Toxic Spans Audio), the first dataset for toxic spans detection in Vietnamese speech, comprising 11,000 audio samples (25 hours) with accurate human-annotated transcripts.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports benchmark results for Vietnamese audio toxic-span detection.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports benchmark results for Vietnamese audio toxic-span detection.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Dataset construction, annotation agreement, language, ASR errors, and social context bound the result; a benchmark score is not a complete safety policy.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Tonal Contrasts in the Malipo Variety of the Mienic Language
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Measure tonal contrasts in the Malipo variety as an object of speech description and evaluation.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Contrastive measurements expose which acoustic distinctions carry linguistic information.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Tonal contrasts are measured from 1,152 recordings by eight Malipo speakers (four male, four female) across test words and repetitions. Tone-bearing-unit F0 contours are Log-Z normalized and duration is measured; linear mixed-effects models use tonal and vowel types as fixed effects and speakers as random effects to compare lexical tone categories.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports an empirical study of tonal contrasts in a Mienic variety.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports an empirical study of tonal contrasts in a Mienic variety.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Speaker sample, elicitation design, tonal context, and language-specific scope bound transfer.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Speech transcription from South Tyrolean Dialect to Standard German with Whisper
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build manually annotated and synthetic dialect data, fine-tune Whisper for the dialect-to-standard text mapping, and evaluate the actual archival translation task.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The paper fine-tunes Whisper for South Tyrolean dialect speech to Standard German text, uses a small manually annotated plus synthetic corpus, and optimizes the task for archival audiovisual material.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: To address an unmet need for subtitling and translation, we introduce a small corpus of manually annotated and synthetic speech data compiled for this task.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports a BLEU score of 86.18 and substantial improvement over its baselines, with an existing heritage-archive use case.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports a BLEU score of 86.18 and substantial improvement over its baselines, with an existing heritage-archive use case.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Small corpus, synthetic data, dialect region, reference translations, BLEU, and deployment domain bound the claim; high translation score does not establish coverage of every speaker or dialect context.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Are You Being Sarcastic? Prosodic Cues to Irony Perception in German
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Vary prenuclear and nuclear accent placement/type and measure regional listeners' sarcasm decisions and response times.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: German utterances are presented in seven prosodic conditions to listeners from Freiburg and Trier, who classify them as sarcastic or sincere.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Participants from two regions in Germany, Freiburg and Trier, listened to short utterances such as Das sieht ja umwerfend aus (“That looks stunning”) in seven prosodic conditions.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Prenuclear accent presence and especially L*+H nuclear accents drive irony judgments; some conditions also yield faster ironic responses.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Prenuclear accent presence and especially L*+H nuclear accents drive irony judgments; some conditions also yield faster ironic responses.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The utterances, regions, prosodic manipulations, and binary judgment task bound the result; other languages and natural conversations remain open.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: A Multimodal Chinese Dataset for Cross-lingual Sarcasm Detection
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Analyze accent robustness under multilingual conditions and identify where recognition errors reflect a narrow training norm.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Subgroup and accent-conditioned evaluation separates intended-word performance across varieties rather than hiding failures in an aggregate.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Sarcasm is expressed through subtle cues like pitch, speech rate, and facial expressions, with patterns varying across languages, e.g., English speakers lower the pitch while Cantonese speakers raise it.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports a study of multilingual/accent robustness and its implications for ASR evaluation.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports a study of multilingual/accent robustness and its implications for ASR evaluation.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Accent labels, languages, speakers, test design, and subgroup denominators bound transfer.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Audio-Based Classification and Geographic Regression of Austrian Dialects
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Use speaker augmentation to reduce speaker-specific bias and jointly examine dialect/location classification with geographic-coordinate regression.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The model learns speech representations for hierarchical classification and a continuous coordinate prediction; held-out speaker and location splits test whether regional structure survives identity variation.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Dialect classification remains challenging due to regional variability and limited dialect-specific datasets.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The Austrian dataset covers 304 speakers at 108 locations; wav2vec 2.0 reports an average geographic test error of 66.7 km in the paper's evaluation.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The Austrian dataset covers 304 speakers at 108 locations; wav2vec 2.0 reports an average geographic test error of 66.7 km in the paper's evaluation.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Sampling density, speaker augmentation, Austrian dialect geography, split design, and recording conditions limit transfer; geographic prediction is not a complete sociolinguistic account of dialect.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Are loan sequences different from foreign sequences? A perception study with Japanese listeners on coronal obstruent – high front vowel sequences
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Compare AX discrimination of a loan-permitted sequence with a prohibited sequence and measure whether individual English exposure explains performance.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Japanese listeners discriminate /ti/ and /zi/ contrasts in an online task; sequence status and self-reported English input are tested as competing explanations.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: This was tested with the native Japanese sequences of palatal affricate plus /i/, compared to /ti/ (accepted only in loanwords) versus /zi/ (not accepted in Japanese) in an online AX discrimination task with 39 Japanese speakers (21-63 years old), who also had to answer three questions on their received English input.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Thirty-nine listeners performed better on the loanword-permitted sequence, though the foreign sequence was also often discriminated; self-reported English input did not explain the result.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Thirty-nine listeners performed better on the loanword-permitted sequence, though the foreign sequence was also often discriminated; self-reported English input did not explain the result.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Online testing, sequence choices, speaker exposure, sample size, and self-report limit generalization; discrimination is not equivalent to lexical access or translation competence.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: On the Relationship between Accent Strength and Articulatory Features
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Use dictionary-based phonetic differences as an accent-strength index and correlate it with articulatory features inferred from acoustic speech.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Self-supervised articulatory inversion estimates tongue and related articulator features; phoneme-level deviations from dictionary references provide the comparison variable across American and British English.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Analyzing a corpus of read speech from American and British English speakers, this study examines correlations between derived articulatory parameters and accent strength proxies, associating systematic articulatory differences with indexed accent strength.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports dialect differences in tongue positioning, especially for rhotic and low-back vowels, and associations between derived articulatory parameters and indexed accent strength.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports dialect differences in tongue positioning, especially for rhotic and low-back vowels, and associations between derived articulatory parameters and indexed accent strength.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Read speech, two dialect groups, dictionary assumptions, inversion error, and correlation do not establish a universal accent scale or causal articulatory explanation.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Lexical competition in the process of Cantonese tone merging: Diverse Impact Mechanisms Across Different Individuals and Tone Pairs
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Examine lexical competition separately for each speaker and tone pair, then relate production distributions to the speaker's merger pattern.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Cantonese tone production is measured for speakers with no clear merger, one merged pair, or multiple merged pairs; lexical competition is compared across pairs.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Cantonese tone-merger analysis uses perceptually selected correct and merged productions from participants, with eight additional participants chosen to balance merger groups. Average pitch, slope, and curvature features for three tone pairs feed Random Forest models separately for competitive and non-competitive lexical contexts; five-fold cross-validation selects tree counts and outputs are checked against perceptual labels and contour divergence. Production accuracy and mixed-effects/GCA models test competition, age, gender, and tone-pair effects, with an 80% threshold defining merger.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: Competition helps maintain contrasts in some speakers, consistently inhibits one pair, has three patterns for another, and has little effect in speakers merging all three tones.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: Competition helps maintain contrasts in some speakers, consistently inhibits one pair, has three patterns for another, and has little effect in speakers merging all three tones.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The Cantonese pairs, speaker groups, lexical measure, and production task bound the result; it is evidence about a change process, not a forecast of every speaker's future pronunciation.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Prosodically Enhanced Foreign Accent Simulation by Discrete Token-based Resynthesis Only with Native Speech Corpora
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Add explicit duration modification to discrete-token resynthesis so native speech can approximate durational foreign-accent cues without accented training data.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Self-supervised discrete units preserve linguistic content, while duration controls alter timing before the units are rendered by a decoder; real L2 speech supplies the comparison target.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: By using the synthesized accented speech as listening materials for humans or training data for automatic speech recognition (ASR), both of them will acquire higher robustness against foreign accents.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports that the enhanced method reproduces durational accents observed in real L2 speech.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports that the enhanced method reproduces durational accents observed in real L2 speech.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Accent languages, speakers, duration estimator, perceptual validation, and native-corpus assumptions bound transfer; acoustic similarity is not proof of improved ASR or pedagogy.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Build a public multi-dataset leaderboard that compares models across dialects and also exposes robustness, adaptation, efficiency, and memory dimensions.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: The benchmark fixes model/data/evaluation axes across six test corpora and records WER plus resource and adaptation measurements.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: In recent years, the enhanced capabilities of ASR models and the emergence of multi-dialect datasets have increasingly pushed Arabic ASR model development toward an all-dialect-in-one direction.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports broad comparative results and identifies differences in dialect robustness, speaker adaptation, inference efficiency, and memory use.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports broad comparative results and identifies differences in dialect robustness, speaker adaptation, inference efficiency, and memory use.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: Corpus selection, language variety, transcription conventions, model versions, and leaderboard maintenance bound the conclusion; rankings are not a causal explanation of dialect performance.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: Tonal Perception in Changde Mandarin
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Measure perceptual cues for all four Changde Mandarin tones and test whether tone continua meet behavioral standards for categorical perception.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Production and perception data examine T1–T4 contours and T2-T3 and T2-T4 continua using tone identification and cue analyses.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Changde Mandarin tone perception is tested in two experiments with 30 participants: Experiment 1 presents 240 randomized [mi] stimuli across four tones and five pitch-register levels, recording identification and reaction time; Experiment 2 has 15 participants in AX and 15 in ABX discrimination tasks over tone continua with repeated randomized stimuli. Identification and discrimination accuracy are modeled against pitch register, slope, and continuum, with post-hoc comparisons distinguishing categorical and gradient perception.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: T1 is high-level, T2 low-rising, T3 falling rather than level, and the T2-T3 and T2-T4 continua do not meet typical categorical-perception standards.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: T1 is high-level, T2 low-rising, T3 falling rather than level, and the T2-T3 and T2-T4 continua do not meet typical categorical-perception standards.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The Changde variety, speakers, stimuli, cue manipulation, and category criteria bound the result; it should not be generalized to Standard Mandarin or all tonal perception.

d3_comparison_matrix.title: The Role of Contextual Variation in Learning Cantonese Tones from Naturalistic Speech
d3_comparison_matrix.central_move: Compare the amount of contextual variation in naturalistic Cantonese speech with which tone contrasts are easier or harder to acquire.
d3_comparison_matrix.mechanism: Naturalistic Cantonese productions are analyzed across six tonal contrasts and compared with existing acquisition findings under the Distributional Learning Across Contexts proposal.
d3_comparison_matrix.evaluation_object: Most research on acquisition of sound categories has focused on simple two-way vowel and consonant contrasts, leaving open how infants learn more complex or tonal contrasts.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_result: The paper reports that contextual variation can predict which Cantonese contrasts are easier or harder to learn when invariant cues are absent.
d3_comparison_matrix.reported_payoff: The paper reports the following payoff at D3 depth: The paper reports that contextual variation can predict which Cantonese contrasts are easier or harder to learn when invariant cues are absent.
d3_comparison_matrix.evidence_limit: The naturalistic corpus, tone system, acquisition comparison, and distributional measures bound the inference; a prediction from correspondence is not a direct infant-learning experiment.

family_synthesis.comparison_conclusion: The papers share the ordinary pressure but intervene at different points in the chain; their reported outcomes are not directly rankable unless the measured object and test condition match.
family_synthesis.named_contrast: Is it all about race?: A Cross-examination of /s/ in a Multilingual (Nigerian) Context versus LID Models are Actually Accent Classifiers: Implications and Solutions for LID on Accented Speech
family_synthesis.mechanism_contrast: Is it all about race?: A Cross-examination of /s/ in a Multilingual (Nigerian) Context addresses the pressure by Acoustic realization is interpreted alongside multilingual context rather than one norm.; LID Models are Actually Accent Classifiers: Implications and Solutions for LID on Accented Speech addresses it by The study compares ECAPA-TDNN, MMS, and GEO systems on several corpora, measures accent-language confusion, reverses chunks, and fuses acoustic and sequence representations.. The shared problem is therefore compatible with more than one intervention point.
family_synthesis.evidence_contrast: The first paper reports The paper reports a contextual analysis of /s/ in a multilingual Nigerian setting.; the second reports Dutch-accented English is called Dutch in 82.6% of errors in one setting; sequence-aware systems reduce this confusion while retaining mainstream performance.. These outcomes should not be ranked unless their data, listeners, metric, and test condition are comparable.
family_synthesis.failure_boundary_contrast: The first paper leaves open: Community, language, sampling, annotation, and interpretation bound transfer.; the second leaves open: Datasets, accent categories, chunking, and aggregation define the result; it diagnoses a shortcut but does not prove cultural neutrality or universal transfer.. Those are evidence boundaries, not proof that either method fails outside the paper.
family_synthesis.transfer_question: What would have to remain invariant for this family to work across a new speaker, language, room, device, or task, and which paper evidence here actually tests that transfer?
family_synthesis.evidence_boundary: The shared story is supported only by the reviewed papers listed here; D2 entries support the problem and stated method, while D3 entries support the reported mechanism and evaluation. It is not a venue-wide prevalence claim.
family_synthesis.unresolved_question: What changes when this move is tested outside the speakers, languages, rooms, devices, or benchmark conditions represented by the 19 D3 paper(s)?

concept_families.definition: Maintain intended-word accuracy across pronunciation patterns that differ from the training majority.
concept_families.boundary: A single pooled error rate cannot show which accents fail or whether adaptation changes identity representation.
concept_families.family_claim: The ordinary pressure is Maintain intended-word accuracy across pronunciation patterns that differ from the training majority. In the reviewed evidence, the family appears as LID Models are Actually Accent Classifiers: Implications and Solutions for LID on Accented Speech: Language identification must preserve language evidence while refusing the shortcut that treats accent as language.; Accent Normalization Using Self-Supervised Discrete Tokens with Non-Parallel Data: Discrete tokens change pronunciation while preserving speaker identity with nonparallel accent data.; The ML-SUPERB 2.0 Challenge: Towards Inclusive ASR Benchmarking for All Language Varieties: The benchmark includes 200+ languages, accents, and dialects so multilingual ASR claims are tested across varieties. It must not be confused with neighboring problems outside this boundary: A single pooled error rate cannot show which accents fail or whether adaptation changes identity representation.
concept_families.unresolved: Whether this concept remains useful outside the reviewed speakers, languages, devices, rooms, and tasks is unresolved; 6 D3 paper(s) provide full-paper evidence.

concept_families.definition: Treat grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and discourse conventions of a variety as part of the language, not merely deviations from a standard.
concept_families.boundary: Dialect labels can be contested and may conflate region, ethnicity, class, and speaker identity.
concept_families.family_claim: The ordinary pressure is Treat grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and discourse conventions of a variety as part of the language, not merely deviations from a standard. records.subtheme_name: What a metric actually measures
records.question: Which human or engineering property is the score standing in for?

family_synthesis.ordinary_pressure: Speech systems are used through microphones, networks, interfaces, policies, and people; a benchmark number is only one observation of that whole chain. The subtheme asks: Which human or engineering property is the score standing in for?
family_synthesis.naive_shortcut: A first attempt would answer the question only with word error versus understanding, but that shortcut misses the boundary: A word metric can miss critical entity errors and can penalize harmless orthographic or dialect differences.
family_synthesis.recurring_move: Across this subtheme, papers make word error versus understanding, quality and naturalness, calibration and selective use explicit rather than treating the speech evidence as one undifferentiated variable. The reviewed full-paper mechanisms instantiate that move in different ways; for example: Combine CLAP similarity with repetition penalties, clipping, and LLM feedback during reward optimization.
subtheme_boundary: A word metric can miss critical entity errors and can penalize harmless orthographic or dialect differences.
A score without listeners, conditions, and target definition cannot support a general quality claim.
Calibration on a held-out sample does not guarantee safety under a new population or distribution.
family_synthesis.tradeoff: The recurring move must preserve the evidence relevant to the named concept without importing a neighboring concept's assumptions; the boundaries below state where that interpretation stops.
family_synthesis.reviewed_variation: Optimizing CLAP Reward with LLM Feedback for Semantically Aligned and Diverse Automated Audio Captioning: Optimizing an automated audio-captioning reward raises the question of whether a metric rewards semantic coverage or merely reference style.; SMARTMOS: Modeling Subjective Audio Quality Evaluation for Real-Time Applications: The paper predicts subjective audio-quality judgments for real-time use, directly addressing the gap between a cheap proxy and what listeners actually report.; Intelligibility Prediction for Time-Modified Speech Signals Using Spectro-Temporal Modulation Features: The captured paper's ordinary problem, mechanism, and reported evaluation directly instantiate word-error-versus-understanding within metrics-and-targets.; Benchmarking and Confidence Evaluation of LALMs For Temporal Reasoning: Confidence evaluation tests whether a spoken temporal-reasoning system knows when its answer is uncertain, not only whether its average score is high.
